result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.min_cost_flow()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Compute minimum cost flow from source to sink. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L33703-L33919){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.min_cost_flow( source, sink, demand=None, capacity=None, cost=None, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Minimum cost flow](/assets/graphs/min-cost-flow.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="The max_flow network with a per-unit cost on each edge, labeled flow/capacity then cost. Sending a demand of 4 from S to T at the lowest cost fills S→A, then splits at A between the cheap detour A→B→T and the direct A→T; the costly S→B stays unused and faded. The card lists flow times cost per edge and the totals: flow 4, cost 14." width="100%"} Every edge has a *capacity* (the most flow it can carry) and a *cost* per unit of flow. This method routes flow from `source` to `sink` so that the total cost is as small as possible. It can either push a fixed amount of flow (`demand=`) or push as much flow as the network can carry and, among all maximum flows, return the cheapest one. Where `max_flow()` only asks "how much can get through?", min cost flow also asks "what is the cheapest way to send it?". That makes it a natural fit for: - transportation and logistics problems (shipping goods from suppliers to customers) - assignment problems (matching workers to jobs at minimum total cost) - routing traffic or data where links have both a bandwidth limit and a price - any planning problem that can be phrased as "move X units through a network cheaply" The algorithm is Successive Shortest Path: it repeatedly finds the cheapest augmenting path in the residual network (using Bellman-Ford, so negative per-unit costs are allowed) and pushes as much flow along it as the bottleneck capacity permits. The graph must be directed. Self-loops are ignored. Every edge is routed on its own, so parallel edges between the same pair of nodes each keep their own capacity and cost (the cheaper one fills first) and `flow_dict` reports each one's flow separately. Edges in opposite directions between two nodes are also independent of each other. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [source]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The node where flow originates, given as an integer node ID or a string label. The node must already exist in the graph. [sink]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The node where flow is absorbed, given as an integer node ID or a string label. Must exist in the graph and be different from `source=`. [demand]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [float | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : The exact amount of flow to send from `source=` to `sink=`. If `None` (the default), the method sends the maximum possible flow and returns the cheapest way of doing so. If a number is given, exactly that much flow is sent at minimum cost; a `ValueError` is raised if the network cannot carry that much. Must be non-negative. [capacity]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Name of the edge attribute holding each edge's capacity. If `None` (the default), each edge's capacity is taken from its `"capacity"` attribute if present, otherwise from the edge weight on a weighted graph, otherwise `1.0`. If a name is given, edges lacking that attribute (or holding a non-numeric value) get a capacity of `1.0`. [cost]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Name of the edge attribute holding the cost per unit of flow. If `None` (the default), each edge's `"cost"` attribute is used. Edges lacking the attribute (or holding a non-numeric value) get a per-unit cost of `1.0`. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [tuple[float, float, dict[int, float]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A tuple containing: (1) `total_flow`, the total amount of flow sent; (2) `total_cost`, the sum over all edges of flow times per-unit cost; and (3) `flow_dict`, a dictionary mapping edge IDs to the flow they carry. Only edges with positive flow appear in `flow_dict`. If no path exists and `demand=` is `None`, the result is `(0.0, 0.0, {})`. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is undirected, `source=` or `sink=` doesn't exist, they're the same node, `demand=` is negative, `demand=` cannot be satisfied, or a cycle whose per-unit costs sum to a negative number is reachable from `source=` (the cheapest flow is then undefined). ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Uses the Successive Shortest Path algorithm with Bellman-Ford relaxation, so negative per-unit costs are permitted alongside the usual non-negative case (a reachable negative-cost cycle raises `ValueError`, since a cheapest path is then undefined). The algorithm runs in $O(V \cdot E \cdot F)$ time in the worst case, where $F$ is the number of augmenting steps. Because it always routes along the *cheapest* residual path from source to sink, the final flow is optimal in total cost for the amount sent. The graph must be directed (call `.to_directed()` first for undirected inputs), and self-loops contribute nothing. Leaving `demand=` at `None` sends the maximum possible flow at minimum cost; setting it to a specific value clamps the total and raises `ValueError` if that demand cannot be met by any admissible flow. ## Examples {.doc-examples} With two possible paths from `S` to `T`, the algorithm prefers the cheaper route through `A` (per-unit cost 2) over the more expensive one through `B` (per-unit cost 3), only using the second path once the first path's capacity is saturated. Here the edge weights act as capacities because no `"capacity"` attribute is present: ::: {#bad7ae33 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=True, weighted=True) .add_nodes(["S", "A", "B", "T"]) .add_edges( [ ("S", "A", {"cost": 1.0}), # capacity 10, cost 1 ("S", "B", {"cost": 2.0}), # capacity 10, cost 2 ("A", "T", {"cost": 1.0}), # capacity 10, cost 1 ("B", "T", {"cost": 1.0}), # capacity 10, cost 1 ], weight=10.0, ) ) total_flow, total_cost, flow_dict = graph.min_cost_flow("S", "T") # Returns (20.0, 50.0): both paths get used once the cheaper one saturates (total_flow, total_cost) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (20.0, 50.0) ``` ::: ::: The third element maps edge IDs to flow. Translating the IDs into endpoint labels shows that every edge carries its full capacity of 10: ::: {#10db9d35 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} { (graph.get_label_from_id(e.source), graph.get_label_from_id(e.target)): f for eid, f in flow_dict.items() for e in [graph.get_edge(eid)] } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` {('A', 'T'): 10.0, ('S', 'A'): 10.0, ('B', 'T'): 10.0, ('S', 'B'): 10.0} ``` ::: ::: Passing `demand` sends exactly that much flow (rather than the maximum possible), which is useful when you have a fixed requirement to satisfy at minimum cost: ::: {#fefe428c .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=True, weighted=True) .add_nodes(["S", "A", "T"]) .add_edges([("S", "A", {"cost": 5.0}), ("A", "T", {"cost": 3.0})], weight=20.0) ) # Send exactly 10 units of flow total_flow, total_cost, flow_dict = graph.min_cost_flow("S", "T", demand=10.0) # Returns (10.0, 80.0): 10 units at a combined per-unit cost of 8 (total_flow, total_cost) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` (10.0, 80.0) ``` ::: ::: Just like `max_flow()`, you can use custom attributes for both capacity and cost instead of the defaults. Here the cheap two-hop route `A -> B -> C` (cost 8 per unit) fills up to its bottleneck of 50 before the pricier direct edge (cost 10) carries the remaining 30: ::: {#6036bdcc .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) .add_edges( [ ("A", "B", {"bandwidth": 100, "price": 5}), ("B", "C", {"bandwidth": 50, "price": 3}), ("A", "C", {"bandwidth": 30, "price": 10}), ] ) ) total_flow, total_cost, flow_dict = graph.min_cost_flow( "A", "C", capacity="bandwidth", cost="price" ) # Returns (80.0, 700.0): 50 units at cost 8 plus 30 units at cost 10 (total_flow, total_cost) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` (80.0, 700.0) ``` ::: ::: This scales naturally to classic transportation problems, like shipping from warehouses to stores at minimum total cost. A super-source feeds the warehouses (edge capacity = supply) and the stores drain into a super-sink (edge capacity = demand): ::: {#d814c3de .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=True, weighted=True) .add_nodes( [ "Source", "W1", # Warehouse 1 "W2", # Warehouse 2 "S1", # Store 1 "S2", # Store 2 "Sink", ] ) .add_edges( [ # Source to warehouses (supply) ("Source", "W1", 50.0, {"cost": 0.0}), ("Source", "W2", 60.0, {"cost": 0.0}), # Warehouses to stores (shipping costs) ("W1", "S1", 100.0, {"cost": 8.0}), ("W1", "S2", 100.0, {"cost": 5.0}), ("W2", "S1", 100.0, {"cost": 4.0}), ("W2", "S2", 100.0, {"cost": 7.0}), # Stores to sink (demand) ("S1", "Sink", 40.0, {"cost": 0.0}), ("S2", "Sink", 50.0, {"cost": 0.0}), ] ) ) flow, cost, assignment = graph.min_cost_flow("Source", "Sink", demand=90.0) # Total shipping cost for meeting the 90-unit demand cost ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` 410.0 ``` ::: :::
